title: Health‑Aware Multi‑Objective Deep Reinforcement Learning for Energy Management of Hybrid PV–Wind–Battery Microgrids

authors.name: Dr. Raden Putra
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Institut Teknologi Bandung

abstract: High penetration of photovoltaic (PV) and wind generation in microgrids increases variability and operational stress on Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). Existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) dispatch strategies tend to optimize short‑term economic metrics and ancillary objectives without explicitly accounting for battery degradation, which leads to reduced lifetime and higher life‑cycle cost. We propose HAMD‑DRL, a Health‑Aware Multi‑Objective Deep Reinforcement Learning framework for hybrid PV–wind–battery microgrids that jointly minimizes annual energy cost and incremental battery degradation. The proposed method formulates a Markov decision process (MDP) integrating PV/wind/load dynamics, BESS operational constraints and an empirical cycle‑ and condition‑dependent aging model. We develop a MO‑DDPG variant with adaptive scalarization and multi‑task transfer learning to produce Pareto front policies. Extensive simulations on an off‑grid rural microgrid testbed with historical weather and load data show that our method achieves an annual cost of USD 8,320 and reduces annual capacity fade to 1.6% (estimated lifetime 12.5 years), outperforming rule‑based, MPC and conventional DRL baselines on cost–lifetime tradeoffs. The framework improves operational robustness under realistic uncertainty and provides deployable policies for field microgrids.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: The rapid expansion of distributed renewable generation, especially photovoltaic (PV) arrays and small wind turbines, is reshaping microgrid architectures for rural electrification and grid‑connected applications alike. These hybrid renewable energy systems (HRES) rely increasingly on Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) to buffer variability, perform peak shaving, enable arbitrage, and provide reliability. In many microgrids the economic value of a BESS is limited not only by capital cost but also by calendar and cycling degradation, which translate into replacement expense and reduced system resilience. As a result, energy management strategies must simultaneously consider operational cost and battery health, particularly for remote or rural off‑grid installations where maintenance is costly and replacement logistics are challenging. This motivates an integrated control approach that balances short‑term economics and long‑term asset life, using data‑driven adaptive policies able to handle nonstationary stochastic inputs such as solar irradiance, wind speed, and load demand.

Recent progress in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has enabled adaptive dispatch and energy management policies that learn from high‑dimensional state spaces and stochastic environments [1][2][3]. DRL methods such as Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) and Twin Delayed DDPG (TD3) have been applied to microgrid dispatch, smart homes with energy storage, and market participation, demonstrating strong performance in cost minimization and renewable utilization under uncertainty [4][5][6]. However, despite this success, most DRL studies prioritize operational economic objectives (cost, revenue, curtailment reduction) or ancillary services provision and rarely incorporate explicit battery aging models in their reward designs [6][8][9]. Conversely, health‑aware DRL research concentrated in vehicular powertrains and hybrid electric vehicles targets thermal safety and instantaneous efficiency, not long‑horizon capacity retention in stationary microgrids [2][3][4][5].

The gap remains wide for a systematic multi‑objective DRL formulation that treats battery lifetime as a first‑class objective for PV–wind–battery microgrids. Prior multi‑objective DRL efforts addressed disparate engineering problems such as aerodynamic blade design [7] and multi‑task transfer in control [11], but trade‑offs between energy cost and degradation in HRES have been largely handled by evolutionary algorithms or scalarized static optimizations rather than learning policies that generalize across seasons and stochastic realizations. Moreover, many prior evaluations omit realistic forecasting uncertainty from weather and price signals, limiting confidence in deployment readiness. The absence of a framework that integrates cycle‑ and condition‑based aging within an MDP, produces Pareto fronts of policies, and validates robustness under realistic uncertainties motivates the present work.

We propose HAMD‑DRL, a health‑aware multi‑objective DRL framework designed to (i) incorporate a lightweight empirical battery degradation model into the MDP, (ii) produce a family of Pareto‑optimal dispatch policies that trade energy cost and battery lifetime, and (iii) improve policy generalization using multi‑task transfer learning across seasonal environments. The main contributions of this work are:
1) We formulate a stationary microgrid MDP for hybrid PV–wind–battery systems that explicitly includes battery health variables and an incremental aging cost term in the reward.
2) We design a MO‑DDPG algorithm with adaptive scalarization and multi‑task transfer to generate Pareto front policies across cost–lifetime tradeoffs.
3) We validate the approach on a realistic off‑grid rural microgrid case using historical weather, load traces, and a lightweight aging model, demonstrating reduced annual capacity loss and competitive annual energy cost compared to rule‑based, MPC, and conventional DRL baselines.
4) We provide analysis of robustness under forecast uncertainty and an ablation study on aging model fidelity and scalarization strategy.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II surveys related work on DRL for energy management, battery health‑aware controllers, and multi‑objective DRL. Section III details the system modeling, MDP formulation, battery aging model, and the MO‑DDPG algorithm. Section IV describes the experimental testbed, simulation setup, baselines, and evaluation metrics. Section V presents results including cost and lifetime tradeoffs, Pareto front analysis, robustness tests, and ablation studies. Section VI concludes with limitations and directions for future work.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section reviews three threads of literature relevant to the present study: DRL for microgrid energy management, health‑aware control for battery systems, and multi‑objective/multi‑task DRL. The review highlights the gap at the intersection of these threads and motivates our integrated health‑aware MO‑DRL approach.

section2a.title: DRL for Hybrid Energy Systems and Energy Storage

content.text: DRL has been applied successfully to various energy management tasks including smart home energy scheduling, grid‑tied battery arbitrage, and hybrid generation dispatch. In microgrid studies, DDPG and TD3 variants have been used to learn continuous control policies that minimize energy cost and curtailment while respecting operational constraints [1][6][9]. For example, Chen et al. [1] applied DDPG to a wind–solar–thermal dispatch problem optimizing fuel cost and emissions, demonstrating the ability to handle high variability and nonconvexities. In smart home settings, DDPG reduced electricity bills using time‑of‑use pricing forecasts [6], while other works studied participation of wind–battery clusters in ancillary service markets for revenue maximization [9]. These works underscore the capability of DRL to address stochastic control with continuous actions; however, they rarely include explicit battery aging in the reward or state, focusing instead on economics and reliability.

section2b.title: Health‑Aware Control and Battery Aging Models

content.text: Battery health‑aware control has been studied extensively in electric vehicles and powertrains where DRL or RL algorithms encourage operation within safe thermal and SOC windows to prevent immediate damage [2][3][4][5]. These works typically design rewards or constraints to penalize high currents or extreme temperatures, improving short‑term robustness. Explicit long‑term lifetime prediction and integration into control remain less common. Battery aging models used in control range from physics‑based electrochemical formulations to lightweight empirical regressions capturing dependence on Depth of Discharge (DoD), current, and temperature [12][13]. For stationary microgrids, computational tractability favors empirical cycle‑counting or semi‑empirical models that predict incremental capacity loss per cycle as a function of DoD and operating conditions. Despite available models, integrating them into DRL rewards for Pareto‑optimal tradeoff learning is underexplored.

The proposed framework builds on lightweight aging models similar to those validated in [12][13], embedding a stepwise degradation cost into the MDP to directly influence policy learning toward lifetime preservation while preserving economic performance.

Multi‑objective DRL seeks to generate policies that trade conflicting goals, often yielding Pareto fronts rather than a single scalar optimum. Approaches include scalarization with fixed weights, adaptive scalarization, and Pareto‑front estimation via population methods [7][11][15]. MO‑DDPG variations have demonstrated promise in engineering design tasks, producing solutions with improved hypervolume and reduced computation compared to evolutionary algorithms [7]. Multi‑task and transfer learning techniques accelerate convergence across related environments and increase generalization, useful for seasonal variations in renewable generation [11]. Multi‑agent DRL has also been applied for decomposed control of complex energy systems, allowing local agents to coordinate for system‑level objectives [8].

Despite these advances, a targeted MO‑DRL solution that integrates battery health as an explicit objective for PV–wind–battery microgrids, and which leverages multi‑task transfer for seasonal generalization, remains absent. This motivates our MO‑DDPG design with adaptive scalarization and transfer learning.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section describes the microgrid testbed, modeling assumptions, MDP formulation, battery degradation model, and the proposed MO‑DDPG algorithm with adaptive scalarization and transfer learning. We adopt a modular design so that the aging model and scalarization strategy can be swapped for different hardware or operator preferences.

content.text: As presented in Fig. 2 the system architecture consists of PV arrays, a small horizontal‑axis wind turbine, a DC collection bus, bidirectional converters to a Li‑ion BESS, an inverter for AC loads, a forecasting server, and the MO‑DDPG controller implemented on an edge server. The proposed module is designed to receive short‑term forecasts (24 h horizon) and state information including $SOC$, $P_{pv}(t)$, $P_{wind}(t)$, $P_{load}(t)$ and local price signals if grid‑connected. The controller outputs continuous actions $a_t$ representing $P_{batt,ch}(t)$ and $P_{batt,dis}(t)$ bounds and curtailment setpoints. The power balance at each time step must hold and is written as a deterministic accounting equation used by the simulator during training and by the real‑time dispatcher at execution.

The microgrid comprises a 70 kWp PV array, a 30 kW wind turbine mounted on a 12 m mast, and a 100 kWh Li‑ion BESS with a modular BMS and a bidirectional 50 kW converter. section3c.title: MDP Formulation and Battery Aging Model

content.text: We formalize the energy management problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) with state $s_t$, action $a_t$, transition $p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)$ and reward $r_t$. The state comprises $s_t = [SOC_t, P_{pv}(t), P_{wind}(t), P_{load}(t), \hat{f}_{weather}(t:t+H), \hat{f}_{load}(t:t+H), t_{hour}]$ where $\hat{f}$ denotes short‑term forecasts over horizon $H$. The continuous action $a_t$ parameterizes battery charge/discharge power setpoints and PV/wind curtailment fractions. The transition uses a digital twin integrating converter dynamics and the battery SOC update. The SOC discrete update follows an energy accounting rule that includes charge/discharge efficiency $\eta_{ch}$ and $\eta_{dis}$. The proposed battery aging model estimates incremental capacity loss per time step using DoD, instantaneous current magnitude $|I(t)|$, and cell temperature $T(t)$, yielding a lightweight but physically interpretable degradation estimate amenable to long‑horizon simulation.

Equation (2) updates the SOC where $E_{rated}$ is the nominal pack energy capacity and $\Delta t$ is the simulation time step (10 s). The charge efficiency $\eta_{ch}$ and discharge efficiency $\eta_{dis}$ capture converter and internal losses. Actions that attempt simultaneous charge and discharge are projected onto admissible domains to avoid infeasible control signals.

Equation (3) provides the incremental capacity fade model per time step where $\mathrm{DoD}(t)$ is the effective depth of discharge for a counted cycle or partial cycle during the interval, $T(t)$ is cell temperature in \degree C, and $I(t)$ is current magnitude. Constants $k_1\text{--}k_4$ are calibrated from laboratory cycle data for the target cell chemistry. The cumulative fade $C_{fade}(t)$ is computed by summation and mapped to State of Health $SoH=1- C_{fade}(t)$ for reporting and reward computation. This lightweight model trades physical completeness for simulation speed suitable for many Monte Carlo runs across multi‑year horizons.

The reward is multi‑component: economic component $R_{cost}$ penalizes grid purchase and curtailment, aging component $R_{aging}$ penalizes incremental capacity loss $\Delta C(t)$, and constraint penalties apply for SOC violations or load shedding. A scalarized reward for training a particular policy is formed using adaptive weights $w = [w_c,w_a,w_p]$ that can be varied to produce a Pareto front of solutions.

content.latex: r_t = -\left(w_c C_t + w_a \Delta C(t) + w_p P_{pen}(t) \right)

content.text: In (4), $C_t$ denotes instantaneous energy cost (USD) computed from grid purchases and curtailment penalties, $\Delta C(t)$ is aging increment from (3), and $P_{pen}$ encodes hard constraint violations. The proposed training uses adaptive scalarization that regularly updates $w_a$ and $w_c$ following operator preference or via an automated scheduler to sample policies across the cost–lifetime Pareto frontier.

section3d.title: Algorithm Design: MO‑DDPG with Transfer and Adaptive Scalarization

content.text: We base the continuous control backbone on DDPG/TD3 actor–critic architectures due to continuous action requirements. The proposed MO‑DDPG extends standard DDPG by training multiple actor–critic pairs under different scalarization weights, combined with an adaptive weight scheduler that moves along a target trade‑off direction to populate the Pareto front efficiently. To improve sample efficiency and generalization across seasons and operating regimes, we implement multi‑task transfer: policies trained on one seasonal environment initialize policies for adjacent seasons and share critic replay buffers selectively. The actor network parameterizes deterministic mapping $\mu_{\theta}(s)$ and the critic estimates $Q_{\phi}(s,a)$.

Equation (5) gives the deterministic policy gradient used to update actor parameters $\theta$. Critic updates minimize a square TD error using target networks. The critic loss used in our implementation follows (6), where $\gamma$ denotes the discount factor and target networks are indicated by primes.

We augment training with prioritized experience replay biased towards transitions with higher $\Delta C(t)$ to accelerate learning of health‑sensitive behaviour. In evaluation, Pareto fronts are extracted by collecting final policies trained under different weight vectors and computing their annualized cost and estimated lifetime using the aging estimator. Algorithmic hyperparameters are provided in Table II. The algorithm is designed to be implementable on edge compute with inference latency under 50 ms, satisfying real‑time dispatch requirements in our testbed.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: We evaluate HAMD‑DRL on a high‑fidelity simulator calibrated to the ITB testbed and on limited hardware‑in‑the‑loop experiments. Experiments cover seasonal weather variability, multiple stochastic seeds, and baselines including rule‑based heuristics, deterministic MPC, and a DRL variant without aging in the reward.

content.text: The simulated microgrid mirrors the hardware specifications in Table I and uses historical weather and load traces for the Bandung region from 2015–2020. Forecasts are produced by LSTM ensembles trained on a three‑year window and updated weekly. The simulation horizon for policy evaluation is 365 days for each Monte Carlo seed, with 100 stochastic replications to estimate uncertainty. The time step is 10 s for power accounting and 1 min for aging accumulation. Key experimental parameters and algorithm hyperparameters are listed in Table II. Final validation on the hardware testbed included 72 hours of controlled dispatch using the deployed policy to verify measurement and control integration.

content.text: We evaluate policies on annualized energy cost (USD/year), estimated annual capacity fade (%/year), and derived estimated lifetime to 80% capacity (years). The evaluation set includes seasonal splits (monsoon, dry season) and unseen stochastic seeds to test generalization. Baselines consist of: a rule‑based heuristic prioritizing SOC corridors and greedy PV utilization; deterministic MPC optimizing a 24 h horizon with cost weights but no aging model; and a DRL policy trained on identical state/action spaces but with $w_a=0$ (no aging reward). For each approach we report mean and standard deviation across Monte Carlo runs.

Table III summarizes key results: the proposed MO‑DDPG policy achieves an annual cost of USD 8,320 and reduces annual capacity fade to 1.6% which translates to an estimated lifetime of 12.5 years to 80% SoH. Compared to DRL non‑health, the proposed method increases annual cost by only 1.46% while more than halving annual capacity fade (4.0% down to 1.6%), supporting H1 stating that health‑aware policies can preserve lifetime with minimal cost penalty. section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: To demonstrate advantages of the proposed multi‑objective formulation, we compare Pareto fronts obtained by adaptive scalarization MO‑DDPG, fixed weighted sum DDPG, and an evolutionary multi‑objective optimizer applied offline to the same digital twin. Fig. 8 shows that MO‑DDPG yields higher hypervolume and more diverse policy solutions for the cost–lifetime tradeoff. Ablation studies include removing the aging term ($w_a=0$), disabling transfer learning, and varying aging model fidelity. Results indicate that (i) removing the aging term causes a substantial increase in annual capacity fade, (ii) transfer learning reduces training time and improves generalization across seasons, and (iii) aging model complexity beyond the semi‑empirical form used yields diminishing returns given forecasting uncertainty.

content.text: As presented in Table IV and Fig. 8, the proposed method achieves an excellent compromise between cost and lifetime. While some offline evolutionary methods can produce slightly lower cost at the expense of higher degradation, MO‑DDPG yields practical online policies that can be deployed with low latency and that explicitly protect battery health. These results corroborate H3 regarding Pareto improvements and H4 on transfer learning benefits.

We performed long‑running endurance simulations spanning 5 simulated years per policy, accelerated in the digital twin by aggregating identical stochastic months to evaluate long‑term fade with Monte Carlo sampling. Stress tests included a sequence of high DoD cycling events, forced depth‑charge sequences, and prolonged temperature elevation to test worst‑case aging sensitivity. The proposed MO‑DDPG policies maintain SOC buffers and curtailment schedules that reduce time spent at extreme DoD values, limiting accelerated aging during stress sequences.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We propose HAMD‑DRL, a health‑aware multi‑objective DRL framework for hybrid PV–wind–battery microgrids that jointly optimizes annual energy cost and battery lifetime. The proposed method integrates a lightweight empirical aging model into the MDP and uses MO‑DDPG with adaptive scalarization and multi‑task transfer learning to produce Pareto‑optimal policies. Extensive experiments using a digitally calibrated testbed and historical weather and load data demonstrate that the proposed controller achieves annualized cost USD 8,320 and reduces annual capacity fade to 1.6%, corresponding to an estimated lifetime of 12.5 years to 80% SoH, while maintaining comparable service levels to cost‑focused baselines. Ablation studies confirm the role of aging reward and transfer learning in improving both lifetime and generalization.

Despite these promising results, limitations exist: the aging model is semi‑empirical and may not capture all electrochemical aging modes under atypical stressors; hardware validation is currently limited to short‑duration deployments due to practical time constraints; and the approach assumes reliable short‑term forecasts which, if severely biased, can affect Pareto performance. Future work includes (1) integrating physics‑informed aging models with online parameter adaptation using field data, (2) extending to multi‑agent formulations for geographically distributed microgrids coordinating through limited bandwidth links, and (3) long‑term field trials to validate lifetime projections and refine economic lifecycle analysis under real replacement schedules and component cost dynamics. We believe the framework opens a practical pathway to deployable health‑aware controllers in rural and grid‑connected microgrids and aligns with priorities for sustainable, resilient renewable energy systems.
